forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
question: How does Handel make trumpets, horns, oboes and strings take turns?
intro: Two trumpets open the suite with a fanfare, and the horns, oboes and strings each take a turn to answer. Follow which group is speaking, and which instruments rest while it does.

sections.label: Trumpets resume after a second pause
The second passage returns
sections.mNote: the music from 0:30 returns fourteen bars later

cues.title: Trumpets call, horns answer
cues.text: Two trumpets sound a fanfare and oboes, violins and viola echo it in quick semiquavers. Around 0:10 the horns take the fanfare alone, with bassoon and continuo running beneath, and the level falls about ten decibels. A half-second silence at 0:18 closes the exchange.
cues.evidence: HHA bars 1–8 and Arnold’s 1788 score, p. 35: the trumpets lead bars 1–5 with oboes, violins and viola echoing them; the horns enter at the end of bar 5 and play to bar 8 with only fagotto and bassi. The first sound is at 1.3 s; the relative level is −7.0 dB at 9.5 s, −17.7 dB at 10.0 s and between −9 and −18 dB to 17.5 s, then −32.9 dB between 17.95 and 18.46 s.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Silence, then another round
cues.text: A second silence at 0:30 opens another round. The trumpets lead, oboes and violins run D major arpeggios while the bass rests, and the horns take their turn. The round returns near 0:59, so the middle of the movement behaves like a ritornello.
cues.evidence: HHA bars 15–21: trumpets lead, then oboes, violins and viola on D major arpeggios with the bass resting (bars 17–18), then horns with fagotto and bassi (bars 19–21); the same passages recur at bars 29–36, the arpeggios at bars 31–32. The level falls to −34.8 dB between 29.98 and 30.60 s, and the level curve for 0:31–0:46 matches 1:00–1:15 at an offset of 29.0 s (correlation 0.93). The bars fall on a steady grid of about 2.06 s a bar, fixed by the pauses at 18.2 and 30.3 s and the entry at 75.6 s.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The whole orchestra enters
cues.text: From about 1:11 the horns play two bars alone. Then, at about 1:15, trumpets, horns, oboes, second violins and viola enter together on one dotted tune, with first violins and the low strings adding running figures; the level jumps about twenty decibels within a fifth of a second.
cues.evidence: The relative level rises from −29.3 dB at 75.51 s to −6.4 dB at 75.70 s. HHA bars 35–36 give the horns, fagotto and bassi alone, beginning near 71.5 s on the steady bar grid of 2.064 s from a first downbeat at about 1.3 s; bar 37 brings in trumpets, horns, oboes, violin II and viola on the tune, with violin I and the bass in running figures. The level then stays between −0.1 and −11.5 dB to 95.3 s, the loudest stretch of the movement.

cues.title: The closing Adagio
cues.text: The last tutti chord stops at about 1:35 and the hall rings for several seconds. From about 1:42 the strings alone play six soft chords roughly three seconds apart, the score’s closing Adagio. The video shows the violins playing; the sound has died away by 2:03.
cues.evidence: The relative level falls from −0.1 dB at 95.3 s to −21.5 dB at 96.0 s. Level peaks follow at 102.0, 105.0, 108.0, 111.0, about 114.5 and 117.5 s (−17.7 to −24.5 dB, against −27 to −36 dB between them), matching the six chords of HHA bars 48–50, a string-only Adagio (Arnold’s 1788 score, p. 39). The official video shows the conductor at about 1:43 and the violin section in close-up from about 1:46 to 2:00. The level is below −40 dB from about 123 s.

transitions.title: A half-second silence ends the horns’ turn
transitions.how: The horns’ restatement of the fanfare, over running bassoon and bass, ends and every part stops for about half a second. Trumpets, horns, oboes, violins, viola and bass then return together with short notes and rising figures, so one group speaking at a time gives way to the whole orchestra. The key signature stays at two sharps; the join is made by the silence and the change of scoring.
transitions.evidence: The relative level falls to −32.9 dB between 17.95 and 18.46 s. Scoring from HHA bars 5–11 and Arnold’s 1788 score, p. 35.

transitions.title: A second silence, then trumpets lead again
transitions.to: Trumpets resume after a second pause
transitions.how: After the exchange of short chords the music stops again, this time for about 0.6 seconds. When it restarts the trumpets lead; then oboes, violins and viola answer with D major arpeggios while the bass rests (bars 17–18), and the horns, bassoon and continuo take their turn (bars 19–21). The movement repeats its plan of silence, one group, then another, with the trumpets now carrying the line.
transitions.evidence: The relative level falls to −34.8 dB between 29.98 and 30.60 s. Scoring from HHA bars 15–21 and Arnold’s 1788 score, pp. 36–37.

transitions.title: The exchange shortens to a bar
transitions.from: Trumpets resume after a second pause
transitions.how: No silence separates these sections. Bar 22 gives the horns one last phrase over running quavers in bassoon and bass; bar 23 hands a short turning figure to trumpets, oboes, violins and viola together, and bar 24 hands it to horns, bassoon and continuo. The two groups now answer one another every bar instead of every few bars, so the pace of the dialogue quickens while the tempo and key signature stay the same.
transitions.evidence: HHA bars 22–24, placed on the bar grid fixed by the measured pauses at 18.2 and 30.3 s and the entry at 75.6 s (about 2.06 s a bar). The level shows no gap here, only a brief dip to −23.9 dB at 46.5 s.

transitions.title: Three short dips lead to the return
transitions.how: Three brief dips in level, about half a second apart at 58.9, 59.4 and 59.95 s, lead into bar 29, where music matching the stretch from bar 15 returns. Trumpets and strings come first, then arpeggios in oboes and violins (bars 31–32) and a turn for horns, bassoon and continuo (bars 33–36) repeat the earlier pattern fourteen bars on, so the middle of the movement behaves like a ritornello that the listener can recognise.
transitions.evidence: Dips to −19.7 to −21.3 dB at 58.86, 59.44 and 59.95 s. The level curve and the pitch-class content of 0:31–0:46 and 1:00–1:15 match closely (offset 29.0 s, correlation 0.93). The arpeggio and horn passages of HHA bars 17–22 recur at bars 31–36.

transitions.title: Horns alone, then everyone at once
transitions.how: Bars 35–36 give the horns, with bassoon and continuo in running quavers, two bars alone while trumpets, oboes and strings rest. In bar 37 trumpets, horns, oboes, second violins and viola enter together on one dotted tune, first violins add semiquaver figures and the bass keeps running. The level rises about 23 dB in under 0.2 seconds, and the music stays at full strength to the close of the tutti.
transitions.evidence: The relative level rises from −29.3 dB at 75.51 s to −6.4 dB at 75.70 s. Scoring from HHA bars 35–38 and Arnold’s 1788 score, pp. 35–39.

transitions.title: Last tutti chord, then strings alone
transitions.how: Bars 45–47 give the whole orchestra a few short chords separated by rests, and the hall rings for several seconds after the last of them. The Adagio then starts with strings and continuo only: six soft chords on the first and third beats of three bars, about three seconds apart, which is roughly three times slower than the Allegro’s crotchet. The oboes, trumpets and horns have finished, and the first violins add sharpened notes (A♯ and D♯).
transitions.evidence: The relative level falls from −0.1 dB at 95.3 s to −21.5 dB at 96.0 s; level peaks at 102.0, 105.0, 108.0, 111.0, about 114.5 and 117.5 s give chord spacings of about 3 s against a crotchet of about 0.5 s in the Allegro. HHA bars 45–50 and Arnold’s 1788 score, p. 39. The official video shows the violins playing at about 1:46–2:00.

source.title: Handel, The Celebrated Water-musick in score (London: Samuel Arnold, 1788), pp. 35–39
source.locator: Commons images 19–21 of 30 (BnF). Parts and the order of passages checked there; bar numbers follow the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Bärenreiter, 1962; IMSLP #559922, printed pp. 39–43), whose repeats and da capo structure the recording matches. The performing edition is not identified and the programme lists no players, so entries show the parts printed in the score; the sound in the horn-only bars (10–18 s, 71–75 s) confirms that horns play, while trumpets and oboes are taken from the score. The closing string-only Adagio is placed from the measured chord attacks and the violin close-ups in the official video; that the harpsichord joins it is assumed from the continuo part. Times follow a steady bar grid and are approximate.

timeline.note: Trumpets give the fanfare; oboes, violins and viola echo it in semiquavers (bars 1–4).
Horns restate the fanfare while bassoon and continuo run beneath; trumpets, oboes and violins rest (bars 5–8).
After the pause every section plays short chords and rising figures (bars 9–11).
One bar for trumpets, oboes and upper strings; horns and bass rest (bar 12).
Horns answer with bassoon and continuo (bars 13–14).
Trumpets restart; strings and bass join in the next bar (bars 15–16).
Trumpets hold a dotted tune while oboes and violins run D major arpeggios; the bass rests (bars 17–18).
Horns again, with bassoon and continuo in running quavers (bars 19–21).
Two groups answer each other in short phrases (bars 23–28); the foreground changes bar by bar.
The earlier pattern returns: trumpets and strings first (bars 29–30).
Arpeggios in oboes and violins under the trumpets’ tune; the bass rests (bars 31–32).
Horns take their turn with bassoon and continuo; they are alone with the bass in bars 35–36 (bars 33–36).
Everyone on one dotted tune; first violins and low strings add running figures (bars 37–47).
The last tutti chord rings in the hall; the score has rests before the Adagio.
Closing Adagio: strings and continuo alone play six soft chords about three seconds apart (bars 48–50); oboes, trumpets and horns rest.
The last chord has died away.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor)
fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. A harpsichord, strings with a double bass, a bassoon and a trumpet are visible in the Marine Band’s video frames; horns and oboes could not be identified there.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (11 of the three suites), the 50 bars and the closing string-only Adagio match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The numbering 11–15 for this suite follows the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962) and IMSLP; other editions may agree. The recording plays the closing Adagio (bars 48–50, strings only): about six soft chord attacks, roughly three seconds apart, follow the last tutti chord, and the official video shows the violins playing at about 1:46–2:00. The stretch is identified from the score, the six level peaks and the video, not by listening; whether anything else is audible after the last chord has not been checked by ear.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.
